title: Sino-Korean Numbers
plainEnglish: The number set borrowed from Chinese — used for dates, money, minutes, phone numbers, and most measured amounts.
whenToUse: Reach for Sino-Korean numbers whenever you read something off a measured scale rather than counting items one by one: dates (삼월 오일 = March 5), money (오천 원 = 5,000 won), minutes (십 분 = 10 minutes), phone numbers (공일공 = 010), floors (삼 층), apartment/room numbers, bus and subway line numbers (이 호선 = Line 2), and any quantity in the hundreds, thousands, or above. The intent is 'I'm naming a number on a system,' not 'I'm tallying objects in front of me.' Mnemonic: if it's written on a price tag, a clock face's minute side, a calendar, or a sign, it's almost always Sino. Example: 1,234 = 천이백삼십사.
attachmentRule: 0 영/공, 1 일, 2 이, 3 삼, 4 사, 5 오, 6 육, 7 칠, 8 팔, 9 구, 10 십, 100 백, 1,000 천, 10,000 만, 억 (100 million). Build by place value: 23 = 이십삼 (2·10 + 3), 405 = 사백오, 30,000 = 삼만. Korean groups large numbers by 10,000 (만), not 1,000.
contrastWith: Sharp contrast vs NATIVE numbers (하나, 둘, 셋…): Sino numbers measure (money, dates, minutes, page/floor numbers), native numbers count discrete things and people. The dividing line is brutal inside one clock phrase — the HOUR takes native but the MINUTE takes Sino, so 7:07 is 일곱(native) 시 칠(Sino) 분, the SAME digit said two different ways. A second contrast: 영 vs 공 for zero — 영 is the abstract math/temperature zero (영 점 = zero point, 영하 = below zero), but in phone numbers and room numbers Koreans say 공 (공일공 = 010). Mixing these (saying 영일영 for a phone number) instantly marks you as a non-native.

examples.en: How much is this? It's 5,000 won.

commonMistakes: Saying 십천 for 10,000 by translating 'ten-thousand' literally — wrong because Korean has a dedicated unit 만 for 10,000, so it is 만 (or 일만). Likewise 100,000 is 십만 (ten 만), not 백천.

Reading minutes with native numbers (서른 분 for 30 minutes) — wrong because 분 'minute' is a Sino counter; the correct form is 삼십 분. (Be careful: 분 meaning 'person/honorific' DOES take native — 두 분 — but the time-unit 분 is Sino.)
Saying 육월 for June and 십월 for October — wrong because of sound-erosion: 6 (육) loses its ㄱ before 월 to become 유월, and 10 (십) loses its ㅂ to become 시월. Every other month is regular (삼월, 칠월, 십일월).
studyOrder: Build tens and hundreds by place value
beginnerExplanation: Korean has TWO number systems, and this is the 'Chinese-origin' one (한자어, literally 'Chinese-character words'). You will use it constantly: every price, date, minute, and phone number is read with these. Learn 일 to 십 first, then 백 (100), 천 (1,000), 만 (10,000). To say bigger numbers you just STACK place values like LEGO bricks: 이십삼 is literally 'two-ten-three' = 23, and 사백오 is 'four-hundred-five' = 405. One big surprise for English speakers: Korean counts large numbers in groups of 10,000 (만), not 1,000. So picture re-drawing the commas every FOUR digits instead of three — 30,000 becomes 삼만 (three 만), and 1,000,000 is 백만 (hundred 만), not 'a thousand thousands.'

title: Native Korean Numbers
plainEnglish: The original Korean number set — used for counting things and people, ages, and the hour of the clock.
whenToUse: Reach for native numbers whenever you are physically tallying discrete items or people in front of you, or stating an age or the hour: counting objects (사과 세 개 = three apples), people (두 명 = two people), animals (한 마리 = one animal), age (스무 살 = 20 years old), and the o'clock hour (네 시 = four o'clock). The intent is 'I'm counting these one, two, three,' not 'I'm reading a number off a scale.' They run 1 to 99 in daily speech; above about 100, even counting switches to Sino (백 개, 이백 명). Mnemonic: if you could point at each thing as you count, it's native.
attachmentRule: 하나 1, 둘 2, 셋 3, 넷 4, 다섯 5, 여섯 6, 일곱 7, 여덟 8, 아홉 9, 열 10; 스물 20, 서른 30, 마흔 40, 쉰 50, 예순 60, 일흔 70, 여든 80, 아흔 90. IMPORTANT: before a counter, 1–4 and 20 shorten: 하나→한, 둘→두, 셋→세, 넷→네, 스물→스무. So 한 개, 두 명, 세 시, 네 살, 스무 살.
contrastWith: Sharp contrast vs SINO numbers (일, 이, 삼…): native = counting/age/hour, Sino = measuring/money/date/minute. The two collide most painfully on the clock: the HOUR is native (다섯 시 = five o'clock) but the MINUTE right after is Sino (오 분 = five minutes). A second contrast English speakers miss — AGE vs YEAR: your age is native (스무 살 = 20 years old) but a calendar year is Sino (이천이십오 년 = the year 2025). Same English word 'year,' two different number systems depending on whether you mean a duration-of-life count (살) or a point on the calendar (년).

examples.en: I'm twenty years old this year.
It's four o'clock now. We leave soon.

examples.ko: 우리 집에 고양이 두 마리 있어요.
examples.en: There are two cats at my place.

commonMistakes: Not shortening before a counter: saying 하나 개 or 셋 시 — wrong because 1–4 and 20 have a special pre-counter shape; the correct forms are 한 개 and 세 시 (and 두 명, 네 살, 스무 살).
Using native numbers for minutes or money (다섯 분, 다섯 원) — wrong because those units are Sino; say 오 분 and 오 원. Native is only for the HOUR (다섯 시), not the minute.
Using Sino for age or the o'clock hour (이십 살, 사 시) — wrong because age and the hour are native; say 스무 살 and 네 시. A learner who says 사 시 will be understood but sounds clearly textbook-wrong.
studyOrder: Memorize 하나~열 then the tens 스물~아흔
Use for things, people, age, and hours
beginnerExplanation: This is the 'home-grown' Korean number set (고유어, 'native words'), and the trickiest thing about it is that 1, 2, 3, 4 — and 20 — change shape right before a counting word. You never say 하나 개; you say 한 개. Think of it like English 'a/an': the number puts on a shorter 'hat' before a counter. Memorize the four little shape-changers as a chant: 한, 두, 세, 네 (and 스무 for 20). You'll use these for counting almost anything you can point at, for your age (스무 살 = 20 years old), and for the hour on a clock (세 시 = three o'clock). Just remember the minute that follows flips back to Sino — 세 시 오 분 (3:05).

title: Telling Time & Dates
plainEnglish: How to read the clock and the calendar — which mixes BOTH number systems in one phrase.
whenToUse: Use this pattern any time you say a clock time or a calendar date. For TIME: the hour is a NATIVE number + 시 (時, 'hour'), the minute is a SINO number + 분 (分, 'minute'); add 반 for 'half past' (두 시 반 = 2:30) and 오전/오후 for a.m./p.m. (오후 세 시 = 3 p.m.). For DATES: year, month, day are all SINO + 년/월/일 (年/月/日), and weekday is 요일 (월요일 = Monday). Intent: you're locating a point on the clock or calendar. Example: 회의가 오후 두 시 반에 있어요 = The meeting is at 2:30 p.m.
attachmentRule: TIME: hour = NATIVE + 시, minute = SINO + 분. 7:07 = 일곱 시 칠 분. 3:30 = 세 시 삼십 분 (or 세 시 반, 'half'). DATE: year/month/day = SINO + 년/월/일. March 5 = 삼월 오일. Two month irregulars: June = 유월 (not 육월), October = 시월 (not 십월). Weekdays: 월·화·수·목·금·토·일 + 요일.
contrastWith: The classic trap is INSIDE one breath: in 일곱 시 칠 분, 시 (hour) takes a NATIVE number but 분 (minute) takes a SINO number — same digit '7,' two different words (일곱 vs 칠). Contrast also 분 the time-unit (Sino: 십 분 = 10 minutes) with 분 the honorific people-counter (native: 두 분 = two persons) — identical syllable, opposite number system. And note the sound-eroded months: 6월 → 유월 and 10월 → 시월 each drop a consonant, while every other month stays regular (삼월, 칠월). For 'o'clock' use 시; do not confuse it with 시간 which means a DURATION of hours (세 시간 = for three hours), not a clock time.

examples.ko: 지금 몇 시예요? 일곱 시 칠 분이에요.
examples.en: What time is it now? It's 7:07.

examples.ko: 회의가 오후 두 시 반에 있어요.

examples.en: It's Friday, so there are a lot of people.

commonMistakes: Saying 칠 시 for 7 o'clock — wrong because the o'clock hour is native; say 일곱 시. (The minute, however, IS Sino: 칠 분.)
Saying 육월 / 십월 for June / October — wrong because these two months erode a sound: June is 유월, October is 시월. The day number stays regular, so June 6 is 유월 육일.
Using a native number for the minute (일곱 분 for '7 minutes') — wrong because 분 is a Sino counter; say 칠 분. Inside 일곱 시 칠 분 you literally switch systems mid-phrase.
beginnerExplanation: Reading a clock in Korean is famously confusing because ONE phrase uses both number systems. The hour is a native number (일곱 시 = seven o'clock) and the minute right after it is a Sino number (칠 분 = seven minutes). So 7:07 is 일곱 시 칠 분 — same digit, two different words! A handy memory hook: the HOUR is the 'pointing/counting' side (native), the MINUTE is the 'measured scale' side (Sino). Dates are all Sino (삼월 오일 = March 5). Just memorize two odd months that swallow a sound: June is 유월 (not 육월) and October is 시월 (not 십월). One more bonus word: 반 means 'half,' so 두 시 반 is a quick way to say 2:30.

title: Counters (Measure Words)
plainEnglish: To count a noun you add a 'counter' word, like 'two CUPS of coffee' — and each counter picks native or Sino numbers.
whenToUse: Use a counter whenever you put a number on a noun. The default order is NOUN + NUMBER + COUNTER: 커피 두 잔 = two cups of coffee, 표 세 장 = three tickets. The counter you choose depends on the noun's shape/type (flat things → 장, cups → 잔, animals → 마리, machines → 대), and that counter in turn fixes whether the number is native or Sino. In casual speech the all-purpose 개 covers most physical objects when you're unsure, but people, animals, and money each demand their own counter. Intent: you're quantifying a specific thing, so you bundle 'how many' with 'what kind of unit.'
attachmentRule: NATIVE-number counters: 개 (things), 명/분 (people; 분 is honorific), 마리 (animals), 살 (age), 시 (o'clock), 장 (sheets), 권 (books), 잔 (cups), 병 (bottles), 대 (cars/machines), 켤레 (pairs), 번 (times). SINO-number counters: 분 (minutes), 원 (money), 월/일/년 (date), 층 (floor), 호 (room), 인분 (food portions), 번 (number/order). Remember 1–4 shorten before native counters (한 개, 두 명, 세 잔).
contrastWith: Sharp look-alike pairs to keep straight: 분 = native 'people/honorific' (두 분 = two persons) BUT Sino 'minutes' (이 분 = two minutes) — same syllable, opposite system. 번 = native 'times/occurrences' (세 번 = three times) BUT Sino 'order/number label' (삼 번 버스 = the No. 3 bus). Also contrast 명 vs 분 for people: 명 is the neutral count (학생 세 명 = three students), 분 is the polite/honorific count for respected adults (손님 세 분 = three guests) — using 명 for your boss's guests sounds cold. English has no counters at all, so the whole system is an added layer: 'two coffees' must become 커피 두 잔, never bare 커피 둘.
commonMistakes: Dropping the counter the way English does ('three apples' → 사과 셋) — wrong because a count needs a counter; say 사과 세 개. Bare 사과 셋 sounds incomplete to a Korean ear.
Using the wrong number system for the counter — e.g. 다섯 분 meaning '5 minutes' (that's the native people-counter); for minutes use Sino: 오 분. Match the system to the counter, not to your habit.
Forgetting to shorten 하나/둘/셋/넷 before native counters (둘 잔, 셋 명) — wrong because 1–4 take their short shape before a counter; say 두 잔, 세 명. This shortening is mandatory, not optional.
studyOrder: Learn the pattern NOUN + NUMBER + COUNTER
Learn which counters take native vs Sino
Always shorten 한·두·세·네 before native counters
beginnerExplanation: In English you can just say 'two coffees,' but Korean almost always slips a 'counter' word in: 커피 두 잔 (coffee + two + cups). Think of it like the obligatory English 'two SHEETS of paper' or 'two HEADS of cattle' — except Korean does it for everything. Different nouns use different counters: 개 for general things, 명 for people, 마리 for animals, 잔 for cups, 장 for flat sheets. The counter also decides whether the number is native or Sino, so they always travel together. Start with the everyday five (개, 명, 마리, 잔, 장) and remember the native numbers shrink in front: 한 개, 두 명, 세 잔. When in doubt about a small object, 개 is your safe default.
